title: What is Epsilon GC (no-op collector), and when is it useful (benchmarking, short-lived programs, allocation-rate analysis)?
shortTitle: What Epsilon GC is: the no-op collector: and when it is useful
keyPoints: Epsilon is a no-op garbage collector that allocates memory but never reclaims it (Java 11, JEP 318).
When the heap is exhausted, the JVM throws OutOfMemoryError or terminates: there is no collection.
Epsilon is ideal for benchmarking because it removes all GC noise from performance measurements.
It measures true allocation rate: run a fixed workload and see how fast the heap fills.
Short-lived programs that finish before the heap fills get maximum throughput with zero pauses.
Epsilon is explicitly NOT for production services; it is a measurement and specialization tool.

s1_definition.oneliner: Epsilon allocates but never collects: the heap only grows until it is full and the JVM stops: and that makes it perfect for benchmarking allocation and running tiny short-lived jobs with zero GC overhead.
s1_definition.profdef:
- **Epsilon GC** – a no-op (passive) garbage collector introduced in Java 11 via JEP 318 that handles allocation but never reclaims memory.
- **No-op collection** – no marking, no relocation, no compaction; the only memory operation is bump-pointer allocation.
- **OutOfMemoryError** – what happens when the heap fills under Epsilon, since nothing can be freed.
- **Benchmarking use** – removing all GC noise to measure the raw cost of code and allocation.
- **Allocation-rate analysis** – running a known workload under Epsilon with a fixed heap to measure bytes allocated per unit of work.
s1_definition.analogy: Epsilon is like a bank that gives out desks to every new customer but never clears any desk. As long as the floor has free desks everything is fast and there is zero cleaning-crew interruption. The moment the floor is full, the bank just closes the doors. You would only run the bank this way to measure exactly how fast desks fill up, or for a pop-up event that you know will end before the floor is full.

sections.s3_flow:
```text
  Epsilon GC lifecycle:
  ─────────────────────────────────────────
  Start: heap is empty
       │
       │  allocate (bump pointer, fastest possible)
       ▼
  ┌───────────────────────────────┐
  │ [obj][obj][obj][obj][obj]...  │
  │ Heap fills from left to right │
  │ Nothing is ever freed         │
  └───────────────────────────────┘
       │
       │  heap full
       ▼
  OutOfMemoryError → JVM stops

  Use cases:
  ┌─────────────────┐  ┌─────────────────┐  ┌─────────────────┐
  │ Benchmarking     │  │ Alloc rate      │  │ Short-lived     │
  │ (zero GC noise)  │  │ measurement     │  │ programs        │
  └─────────────────┘  └─────────────────┘  └─────────────────┘
```
sections.s6_takeaway:
Epsilon is the no-op garbage collector: it allocates by bumping a pointer and never reclaims anything. There are no GC threads, no barriers, and zero pauses. When the heap fills, the JVM throws OutOfMemoryError. It is an experimental collector enabled behind an unlock flag, meant for measurement, not production.

The three legitimate uses are benchmarking (removing all GC noise from measurements), allocation-rate analysis (measuring bytes per operation by watching how fast a fixed heap fills), and short-lived programs that finish before the heap would fill. It also exposes memory leaks fast because nothing is ever freed.

At National Bank of India, Epsilon measured the interest-calculation routine's allocation rate, revealing unnecessary intermediate objects. The team optimized and then ran production under G1.

Remember one sentence: Epsilon allocates but never collects, which makes it the perfect laboratory instrument for measuring allocation, but never the right choice for a service that must run longer than its heap can hold.
